## The data

The 1986 Medicaid Consumer Survey studied adults eligible for Medicaid in Santa Barbara
and Ventura counties, California. One group was enrolled in a managed-care demonstration
program; a comparison group stayed in fee-for-service Medicaid. Each row is one person.
Enrollment was **not** randomized.

| Column | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `id` | Row number |
| `visits` | Number of doctor visits during the observation period |
| `days` | Length of the observation period, in days (32 to 120; 99% of people were observed for at least 89 days) |
| `managed_care` | `yes`: enrolled in the managed-care program; `no`: fee-for-service comparison group (reference) |
| `eligibility` | Medicaid eligibility group: `AFDC` (Aid to Families with Dependent Children; reference) or `SSI` (Supplemental Security Income) |
| `gender` | `female` (reference) or `male` |
| `age` | Age in years. The groups do not overlap in age: AFDC members are 16 to 64, SSI members 65 to 105 |
| `health_pc1`, `health_pc2` | First and second principal-component scores of three health-status measures (functional limitations, acute conditions, chronic conditions). The documentation does not say which direction means worse health, so use them only as adjustment variables |
| `access` | Availability of health services, from 0 (low) to 1 (high) |

*Source:* Gurmu S (1997). Semi-parametric estimation of hurdle regression models with an
application to Medicaid utilization. *Journal of Applied Econometrics* 12, 225–242. Data
from the Journal of Applied Econometrics Data Archive.

## Setup

This chunk loads the same packages as Homework 2 and reads the data. **Do not modify it.**

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(faraway)
library(MASS)              # glm.nb(), polr()
library(pscl)              # zeroinfl(), hurdle()
library(nnet)              # multinom()
library(ResourceSelection) # hoslem.test()
library(sandwich)          # sandwich standard errors
library(lmtest)            # coeftest()
library(VGAM)              # loaded after lmtest, so lrtest() is VGAM's. To compare two
                           # glm() fits, write lmtest::lrtest() or use anova().
select <- dplyr::select    # MASS also has a select(); use the dplyr one

# The CSV must be in the same folder as this file.
if (!file.exists("medicaid-visits.csv")) {
  stop("medicaid-visits.csv not found. Put it in the same folder as this file, ",
       "and set the working directory to that folder ",
       "(RStudio: Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location).")
}
med <- read.csv("medicaid-visits.csv") %>%
  mutate(managed_care = factor(managed_care, levels = c("no", "yes")),
         eligibility  = factor(eligibility, levels = c("AFDC", "SSI")),
         gender       = factor(gender, levels = c("female", "male")))
glimpse(med)
```

## Function reference

Each function you may need, with one example call. The example calls use placeholders
(`<family>`, `<link>`, `<expression>`, `<test>`); choosing what goes there is part of the
exam.

| Function | What it does | Example call |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `glm()` | Fits a generalized linear model | `glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = <family>(link = "<link>"), data = d)` |
| `offset()` | Adds a term to the linear predictor with its coefficient fixed at 1 | `y ~ x1 + x2 + offset(<expression>)` |
| `summary()` | Coefficient table, deviance, dispersion | `summary(m)` |
| `coef()`, `exp()` | Coefficients; exponentiate them | `exp(coef(m))` |
| `confint()`, `confint.default()` | 95% confidence intervals (profile likelihood; Wald) | `exp(confint(m))` |
| `deviance()`, `df.residual()` | Residual deviance and its degrees of freedom | `deviance(m) / df.residual(m)` |
| `residuals()` | Residuals of a chosen type | `residuals(m, type = "pearson")` |
| `update()` | Refits a model with one argument changed | `update(m, family = <family>)` |
| `formula()` | The model formula, including any offset term; can be passed to another fitting function | `formula(m)` |
| `glm.nb()` (MASS) | Fits a negative binomial GLM with a log link | `glm.nb(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d)` |
| `AIC()` | AIC of fits that have a likelihood | `AIC(m1, m2)` |
| `coeftest()` (lmtest), `sandwich()` | Coefficient tests with sandwich standard errors | `coeftest(m, vcov = sandwich)` |
| `anova()`, `lmtest::lrtest()` | Compare nested fits | `anova(m1, m2, test = "<test>")` |
| `predict()` | Predictions, optionally for new data | `predict(m, newdata = nd, type = "response")` |

## Task 1: Choose and fit the model (15 points)

*If your code does not run, write in words what you would fit or compute and why; that earns partial credit.*

The question is how the number of doctor visits relates to managed-care enrollment,
adjusting for eligibility group, the two health scores, gender, age and access. People were
observed for different lengths of time.

**(a)** *(10 points)* Fill in the three blanks below with your choices of family, link and
offset, remove the `#` signs, and run the chunk. Keep the name `m1`; later tasks use it.

```{r}
#| label: task1
 m1 <- glm(visits ~ managed_care + eligibility + health_pc1 + health_pc2 +
             gender + age + access + offset(log(days)),
           family = poisson(link = "log"),
           data = med)
summary(m1)
```

**(b)** *(5 points)* Explain why each of your three choices (family, link, offset) suits
these data. One or two sentences for each is enough.

*Your answer to 1(b):* Poisson: because visits is a non negative cout. Log link gives positive expected counts. We use offset to account for different lengths of observations. 

## Task 2: Check the stated assumption and decide (15 points)

*If your code does not run, write in words what you would fit or compute and why; that earns partial credit.*

A Poisson model assumes that, for people with the same predictor values and observation
period, the variance of `visits` equals its mean. Run the chunk below without changing it.
It computes two checks of this assumption for `m1` and compares its model-based standard
errors with sandwich standard errors. This chunk and the Task 3 chunks run only once `m1`
exists: if they show no output after you render, check that your Task 1 chunk ran.

```{r}
#| label: task2
#| eval: !expr exists("m1")  # runs once the Task 1 model exists
c(deviance = deviance(m1), df = df.residual(m1),
  ratio = deviance(m1) / df.residual(m1))
pearson <- sum(residuals(m1, type = "pearson")^2)
c(pearson = pearson, ratio = pearson / df.residual(m1))
coeftest(m1)                     # model-based standard errors
coeftest(m1, vcov = sandwich)    # sandwich standard errors
```

**(a)** *(5 points)* What do the two ratios show? Is the assumption reasonable for these
data? Cite the numbers. (Two or three sentences.)

*Your answer to 2(a):* The deviancedf ratio=3.06, the chisquaredf ratio is 4.35. Both are greater than 1 it shows overdispersion. No the Poisson asumption of equal meana nd variance is not reasonable for this 

**(b)** *(10 points)* Compare the model-based and sandwich standard errors and p-values for
`managed_careyes`. Why do they differ, and which result would you rely on for the
managed-care question? (Three or four brief points.)

*Your answer to 2(b):* They differ since Model SE=0.0469 p=0.0197.sandwich SE=0.1113 p=0.3256. Overdispersion made model SE too small. I would rely on sandwich result. The managedcare association is not statistically significant.

## Task 3: Refit and compare (15 points)

*If your code does not run, write in words what you would fit or compute and why; that earns partial credit.*

The chunk below is a worked example. It refits your Task 1 model as quasi-Poisson;
`update()` keeps the formula, offset and data the same.

```{r}
#| label: task3-example
#| eval: !expr exists("m1")  # runs once the Task 1 model exists
m_qp <- update(m1, family = quasipoisson)
summary(m_qp)
```

**(a)** *(5 points)* Now fit a negative binomial model with the same predictors and the
same offset, and name it `m_nb`. `update()` cannot make this change: the negative binomial
is fitted by a different function, `glm.nb()`, which has no `family` argument. See the
`glm.nb()` and `formula()` rows of the function reference. One line fits it; you may also
print `summary(m_nb)`.

```{r}
#| label: task3a
m_nb <- glm.nb(formula(m1), data = med)
summary(m_nb)

```

**(b)** *(5 points)* Run the chunk below, which lines up the `managed_careyes` row from the
three models and gives the AIC of the two likelihood-based fits. How does the conclusion
about managed care change from the Poisson fit to the two refits, and why? (Two or three
sentences.)

```{r}
#| label: task3b
#| eval: !expr exists("m1")  # runs once the Task 1 model exists
cmp <- rbind(Poisson = coef(summary(m1))["managed_careyes", ],
             quasi   = coef(summary(m_qp))["managed_careyes", ],
             negbin  = coef(summary(m_nb))["managed_careyes", ])
colnames(cmp) <- c("Estimate", "Std. Error", "z or t value", "p-value")
cmp
AIC(m1, m_nb)   # quasi-Poisson has no likelihood, so no AIC
```

*Your answer to 3(b):* managed care is significant under Poisson (p=0.0197), but not under quasi-Poisson (p=0.2641) or negative binomial (p=0.1869). refits show ooverdispersion. standard errors increased but the estimated association about same. AIC is lower for negative binomial.

**(c)** *(5 points)* Which refit, quasi-Poisson or negative binomial, would you use for Task
4, and why? Give at least one reason, from the output above or from what each model
assumes about the variance. (Two sentences.)

*Your answer to 3(c):* I would use negative binomial model for overdispersion. Lower AIC is also one of teh reasons we can choose negative binomial


reader.

*Your answer to 4(a):* managedcare had an estimated 11.1% lower doctorvisit rate than feeforservice participants RR = 0.889(0.747–1.057). the association is not statistically significant.
